Derisive means showing mocking contempt toward someone or something — treating them as if they are stupid, worthless, or ridiculous, and making that feeling obvious through your words, laughter, or expression.

When you are derisive, you are not just disagreeing with someone. You are laughing at them, looking down on them, and making it clear you find them beneath serious consideration.

Derisive is actually made of two things working together:

1. Mockery — making fun of someone, treating something as a joke.

2. Contempt — a deep sense that something or someone is inferior, unworthy, or laughable.

Take away the contempt, and you just have playful teasing. Take away the mockery, and you just have quiet disrespect. Derisive is when both are present at once — when someone openly, almost gleefully, treats another person or idea as a joke.

The word "derisive" can describe many things — not just a person, but the way a person expresses this attitude:

  • A derisive laugh — a sharp, scornful laugh that signals "I find this ridiculous." It is not a warm or joyful laugh. It is the kind of laugh that makes the other person feel small.
  • A derisive comment — a remark designed to mock and dismiss. For example, if someone shares a business idea and another person says, "Oh sure, and maybe you'll fly to the moon too," that is a derisive comment.
  • A derisive tone — the way something is said, dripping with scorn, even if the words themselves seem neutral. The contempt comes through in the voice.
  • A derisive look — a facial expression — often a smirk, an eye-roll, or a sneer — that communicates the same mocking contempt without any words at all.
  • A derisive attitude — a general approach toward a person or topic that is dismissive and full of ridicule.

The crowd gave a derisive laugh when the politician made his promise.

Here, the crowd is not just laughing — they are laughing at the politician, showing they find his promise foolish or dishonest.

She spoke in a derisive tone when discussing her rival's work.

She didn't just disagree. She mocked it — her tone made clear she thought little of it.

He gave a derisive snort when I suggested we try the new restaurant.

A snort of mockery — quick, dismissive, and designed to make you feel like your idea was silly.

The experienced chef was derisive about the cooking show's techniques.

He didn't politely critique — he mocked them, treating them as unworthy of serious respect.

Imagine someone has just said something. A derisive person does not respond with serious disagreement or polite correction. Instead, they react as if they cannot believe someone could say something so foolish. There is an element of performance to it — the derisive person often wants others to see their scorn. It is contempt worn openly, even proudly.

This is why derisive behavior feels so cutting to the person on the receiving end. It does not just reject your idea — it makes you feel stupid or inferior for having had it.
How Derisive Differs From Similar Words

These words are close in meaning, but each has a slightly different flavor:

  • Mocking is the broad act of making fun of someone. Derisive is a type of mocking that specifically carries heavy contempt and dismissiveness. All derisive behavior is mocking, but not all mocking is derisive (friendly teasing, for instance, is mocking without contempt).
  • Sarcastic means saying the opposite of what you mean, often to mock. A sarcastic person might say, "Oh, brilliant idea." A derisive person might instead just laugh scornfully and say, "That's the most ridiculous thing I've ever heard." Sarcasm is a tool; derisive is an attitude.
  • Scornful is very close to derisive, but scorn can be quiet and internal. Derisive tends to be more expressed and outward — it is scorn that is actively shown and directed at someone.
  • Dismissive means brushing something off as unimportant. Derisive takes it further — it does not just ignore your point, it laughs at your point.
  • Condescending means talking down to someone as if they are inferior. Derisive also looks down, but adds active mockery on top.

Derisive sits on the stronger, harsher end of the spectrum. It is not mild teasing. It carries real sting — the clear intention to make someone feel foolish, small, or unworthy. When you describe someone's behavior as derisive, you are signaling that their mockery was pointed, deliberate, and contemptuous — not gentle or accidental.

Being on the receiving end of derisive behavior is unpleasant and often humiliating. Because derisive mockery is open and outward, it frequently happens in front of others, which adds a layer of public embarrassment. It signals to everyone around that the derisive person does not merely disagree — they consider you or your idea beneath respect.

If you want to remember the word in one clean line:

Derisive = openly mocking and contemptuous — treating someone or something as laughable and unworthy.
